1.blurb: The Ming story of the same fleets, from the other side: the admiral Zheng He's seven giant treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean in the 1400s, the largest the world had yet seen — and the court argument over cost, eunuch power, and Confucian disapproval that made China fold up its sails and walk away from the sea just as Portugal was creeping out onto it.

3.blurb: The West African gold power the Portuguese were trying to reach by sea. At its height under Mansa Musa in the 1320s, Mali was so rich that his pilgrimage to Mecca — handing out gold all the way across the Sahara and Egypt — reportedly crashed the price of gold in Cairo for years.

The largest state in African history, swallowing the fading Mali as the Portuguese arrived on the coast. Under the pilgrim-king Askia Muhammad it ruled the great bend of the Niger, the gold trade, and the scholarly city of Timbuktu — the inland wealth the European voyages were racing to tap from the sea.

The trade that began on this Portuguese dock told from its own narrative: how the sugar-and-slavery model first fused on the Atlantic islands, then scaled across the ocean into the largest forced migration in human history, carrying more than twelve million Africans to the Americas.

7.blurb: The same arrival seen from the African shore. The Swahili city-states — Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi — were wealthy, stone-built, Muslim trading towns plugged into the Indian Ocean economy for centuries before da Gama. Their narrative tells the Portuguese storm from the coast's side: the sack of Kilwa and Mombasa and the long century of ruin that followed the cannon.

8.blurb: Magellan crossed the Pacific chasing the same spices and silver economy that, a generation later, would tie China to the Americas. The Ming narrative tells how the Single Whip tax reform made silver the basis of Chinese money, pulling American silver across the Pacific through Manila and weaving the last gap in the global web shut.

9.blurb: The fall of Tenochtitlan told from the Mexica side. Their narrative carries the empire from its founding on the lake to this last chapter — the floating capital, the tribute system, the human sacrifice, and the collapse under smallpox and the rage of the subject peoples the Mexica had themselves oppressed.

10.blurb: The Andean empire's own story of the catastrophe that preceded the Spanish: smallpox racing south through trade contacts a full eight years ahead of Pizarro, killing the emperor Huayna Capac and his heir and touching off the civil war that left the empire fatally divided when the conquerors finally walked in at Cajamarca.

14.blurb: The horror at the center of the triangular trade, given its own full reckoning: the Middle Passage as a world of its own — the packed holds, the months at sea, the more than a million who died in the crossing — the human core of the system this chapter can only summarize.

Where the casta hierarchy and the resentments of colonial Spanish America finally detonate. Three centuries after the conquest, Spanish-born rulers lording it over American-born whites — with everyone else slotted below by blood — helped blow the empire apart in the wars of independence, whose narrative opens on exactly this pressure cooker.
